q: Its source is Lake Tear of the Clouds in the Adirondack Mountains. The Palisades line its western bank, and it flows past Albany and West Point. It meets the Atlantic at New York Harbor, and the Erie Canal connects to it. For 10 points, name this river that names a school of landscape painters.

Spiral Jetty, an earthwork by Robert Smithson, juts into this lake. It is a shrinking remnant of the ancient Lake Bonneville and has no outlet. Antelope Island lies in it, and brine shrimp live in its extremely salty water. For 10 points, name this lake in Utah near a namesake city.

The Kissimmee River feeds this lake, which is encircled by the Herbert Hoover Dike. Its overflow historically drained south into the Everglades. Towns such as Clewiston and Belle Glade lie on its shores. For 10 points, name this large lake in south central Florida.

Badwater Basin, at 282 feet below sea level, is the lowest point in North America and lies in this place. Furnace Creek is a settlement within it. It is a national park in the Mojave Desert region of California and Nevada. For 10 points, name this extremely hot and dry valley.

The Susquehanna River is the largest tributary of this estuary. Annapolis and Baltimore lie on it, and the Bay Bridge crosses it in Maryland. The Delmarva Peninsula separates it from the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this large bay famous for its blue crabs.

The Appalachian Trail runs from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Mount Katahdin in Maine along this range. Mount Mitchell in North Carolina is its highest peak. The Blue Ridge and the Great Smoky Mountains are parts of it. For 10 points, name this mountain system of the eastern United States.

The Unangan people are native to this volcanic chain, where Shishaldin and Makushin are active volcanoes. Dutch Harbor is a major fishing port here. Japan invaded Attu and Kiska in 1942. For 10 points, name this Alaskan island chain that separates the Bering Sea from the Pacific.

Old Faithful is a geyser in this national park, which sits on a large volcanic caldera. It lies mostly in Wyoming and extends into Montana and Idaho. It was established in 1872. For 10 points, name this national park, known for bison and geysers.

The Pilgrims first landed at Provincetown on this Massachusetts peninsula. A canal cuts across its base, and Hyannis lies on its southern coast. It is shaped like a bent arm, and glaciers formed its many kettle ponds. For 10 points, name this peninsula east of Boston.

Mauna Kea and Kilauea are volcanoes on the largest island of this state. Honolulu is on its island of Oahu, and Maui is the second largest island. It was admitted to the Union in 1959. For 10 points, name this Pacific island state.

Paradise is a visitor area on this peak, which has more glaciers than any other mountain in the contiguous United States. It is a stratovolcano in the Cascade Range. Tacoma lies near its base. For 10 points, name this mountain in Washington State.

Gary, Indiana, and Green Bay, Wisconsin, lie on its shores, and the Sleeping Bear Dunes rise from its eastern side. The Door Peninsula separates it from Green Bay. The Straits of Mackinac connect it to Lake Huron, and Chicago sits at its southwestern corner. For 10 points, name this Great Lake.

Its civil divisions are called parishes rather than counties. Baton Rouge is the capital, and Lake Pontchartrain is north of New Orleans. The United States acquired it in a purchase from France in 1803. For 10 points, name this state with a Cajun culture.

Center-pivot irrigation drawn from this aquifer turned the High Plains into farmland. It underlies parts of eight states, including Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas. Pumping has depleted it faster than rainfall recharges it. For 10 points, name this large underground water source beneath the Great Plains.

This transform fault marks the boundary between the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake occurred along it. The Carrizo Plain shows its trace, and the town of Parkfield sits on it. For 10 points, name this California fault.

Marjory Stoneman Douglas called this wetland a "river of grass." Sawgrass marshes and mangroves here are home to alligators and the Florida panther. It lies southwest of Miami and shares a region with Big Cypress. For 10 points, name this Florida national park.

Saguaro cacti are the signature plants of this desert. It spans southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico, with Phoenix and Tucson in it. The Gulf of California borders it on the south. For 10 points, name this desert.

Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through this pass in the Cumberland Mountains. It lies where Kentucky, Tennessee, and Virginia meet. Settlers used it to cross the Appalachians to the west. For 10 points, name this historic mountain passage.

Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico meet at a single point in this region. A monument marks the exact spot, and visitors can stand in four states at once. The Navajo Nation manages the site. For 10 points, name this region of the Southwest.

This peninsula is shared by Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia. Its name is a blend of those three states. The Chesapeake Bay lies to its west and the Atlantic Ocean to its east. For 10 points, name this peninsula.

Joshua trees grow in this desert, which lies mostly in southeastern California. Barstow and Las Vegas lie near it, and the national preserve here includes Kelso Dunes. Death Valley lies on its northern edge. For 10 points, name this desert.

Seattle and Tacoma lie on this inlet of the Pacific Ocean. The Strait of Juan de Fuca connects it to the ocean, and the Olympic Peninsula forms its western shore. It was named for a lieutenant on George Vancouver's expedition. For 10 points, name this Washington sound.

Emerald Bay is part of this lake in the Sierra Nevada. It is famous for its clarity and straddles the border of California and Nevada. The Truckee River flows out of it. For 10 points, name this large alpine lake.

This peak in the Alaska Range rises 20,310 feet and is the tallest mountain in North America. It lies in a national park of the same name. It was officially renamed in 2015 from a name honoring a president. For 10 points, name this Alaskan mountain.

q: Lake Nasser, created by the Aswan High Dam, lies on this river. Its two main branches, the Blue and the White, meet at Khartoum. Luxor and Cairo lie along it. For 10 points, name this river that empties into the Mediterranean Sea in a large delta.

The Rio Negro meets the Solimoes near Manaus to form the main stem of this river. Its basin holds the world's largest tropical rainforest. It rises in the Andes of Peru and crosses Brazil. For 10 points, name this South American river.

Annapurna and Kangchenjunga are among the peaks of this range, which formed from the collision of India with Eurasia. It runs through Nepal, Bhutan, and Tibet. Mount Everest is its best-known summit. For 10 points, name this mountain range of Asia.

The Tuareg are traditional nomads of this desert, which stretches across Libya, Algeria, and Egypt. The Atlas Mountains lie to its northwest. The Sahel borders it on the south. For 10 points, name this largest hot desert, in northern Africa.

Irkutsk lies near this lake in southern Siberia. Its outflow is the Angara River. The nerpa, a freshwater seal, lives in it, and it holds the greatest depth of any lake. For 10 points, name this Russian lake.

Its source is near Donaueschingen in the Black Forest of Germany. It flows through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. The Iron Gates gorge lies on it, and its delta in Romania meets the Black Sea. For 10 points, name this European river.

Aconcagua is the highest peak of this mountain range, which runs along the western edge of South America. Machu Picchu is among the Inca ruins in it. It passes through Chile, Argentina, Peru, and Bolivia. For 10 points, name this range.

Uhuru Peak is the summit of this volcano, which has three cones named Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira. Glaciers on its snowy top lie near the equator. It is in Tanzania. For 10 points, name this tallest mountain in Africa.

The Rock of Gibraltar looms over this narrow waterway. Spain lies to its north and Morocco to its south. It links the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea. For 10 points, name this strait, whose name is the same as a British territory.
This strait divides the European and Asian parts of Istanbul. It links the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara. Two suspension bridges span it. For 10 points, name this Turkish strait.

This river rises on the Tibetan Plateau and forms part of the border between Laos and Thailand. Phnom Penh sits where it meets the Tonle Sap. Its delta in southern Vietnam is a major rice-growing area. For 10 points, name this river of Southeast Asia.

Varanasi is the holiest city on this river for Hindus. It begins at the Gangotri Glacier and flows across northern India. It joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh to form a vast delta on the Bay of Bengal. For 10 points, name this sacred river.

This structure lies in the Coral Sea off the coast of Queensland. It consists of thousands of individual reefs and islands. Cairns is a common starting point for visitors. For 10 points, name this reef system off Australia.

The Perito Moreno Glacier and Torres del Paine are in this region at the southern end of South America. It is shared by Argentina and Chile. Tierra del Fuego lies at its southern tip. For 10 points, name this windswept region of steppe.

Chile contains this desert, among the driest places on Earth outside the polar regions. It was once a major source of nitrate mining. The ALMA observatory sits at high elevation in it. For 10 points, name this South American desert.

The Jordan River flows into this lake, which borders Israel and Jordan. Its shoreline is the lowest land elevation on Earth. Its salinity is so high that swimmers float easily. For 10 points, name this lake.

Lemurs live only on this island, whose capital is Antananarivo. The Mozambique Channel separates it from the African mainland. Baobab trees line a famous avenue here. For 10 points, name this large island nation in the Indian Ocean.

Thingvellir National Park here marks where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level. Reykjavik is its capital, and the Vatnajokull ice cap covers much of it. Eyjafjallajokull is a volcano here. For 10 points, name this North Atlantic island country.

Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across this river. Boyoma Falls and Livingstone Falls interrupt its course. It crosses the equator twice. For 10 points, name this river of central Africa, which flows through a rainforest to the Atlantic.
The Lorelei is a rock on this river in Germany. It begins in the Swiss Alps and passes Basel and Cologne. It reaches the North Sea at Rotterdam. For 10 points, name this European river.
Speke named this lake for a queen. Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania share it, and Jinja lies where the Nile leaves it. Entebbe is on its shore. For 10 points, name this largest lake in Africa.

Baku lies on the shore of this sea, and the Volga River flows into it. Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, and Russia border it. It is the largest enclosed inland body of water. For 10 points, name this sea.

Challenger Deep lies in this trench in the western Pacific. It is near the island of Guam. It formed where the Pacific Plate subducts beneath another plate. For 10 points, name this deepest known part of the ocean.

Gatun Lake and the Culebra Cut are parts of this waterway, which opened in 1914. A system of locks lifts ships over the isthmus. It links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. For 10 points, name this canal.
Ferdinand de Lesseps led the building of this canal, which opened in 1869. Port Said lies at its northern end. It links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. For 10 points, name this Egyptian canal.

Its capital Nuuk was once called Godthab. Thule Air Base, a United States military installation, lies in its northwest. An ice sheet covers most of this autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. For 10 points, name this large Arctic island.

The Yangtze, Yellow, and Mekong Rivers all begin on this high region. Lhasa lies on it, and it is called the Roof of the World. Qinghai Lake is at its northeastern edge. For 10 points, name this high plateau in central Asia.

Sossusvlei lies in this desert, which has some of the tallest dunes in the world. Welwitschia plants grow here, and the Skeleton Coast lies at its northern edge. It runs along the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa. For 10 points, name this desert in Namibia.

Yekaterinburg lies at the eastern foot of these mountains. Magnitogorsk is an industrial city on them. They are traditionally taken as part of the boundary between Europe and Asia. For 10 points, name this Russian mountain range.

The Uros people live on floating islands of reeds in this lake. Puno, Peru, is on its shore, and the lake lies on the Altiplano. Bolivia and Peru share it, and it is a very high-altitude lake. For 10 points, name this lake of the Andes.

q: In 1676 this Virginia planter led frontiersmen against Native Americans without the approval of Governor William Berkeley. His followers burned Jamestown. He died of dysentery and the revolt collapsed. For 10 points, name this rebellion, named for its leader.

In 1735 Andrew Hamilton won the acquittal of a New York printer on charges of seditious libel by arguing that truth is a defense. The case helped establish freedom of the press. The defendant published the New-York Weekly Journal. For 10 points, name this printer, tried for criticizing Governor William Cosby.

At a 1754 congress in this New York city, Benjamin Franklin proposed a plan of colonial union and published the "Join, or Die" cartoon. Delegates from seven colonies approved it, but no colonial legislature accepted it. For 10 points, name this plan, named for the city.

After the French and Indian War, King George III issued this 1763 order forbidding colonial settlement west of the Appalachian crest. It angered colonists and speculators. For 10 points, name this royal proclamation.

Roger Sherman of Connecticut proposed this 1787 deal at the Constitutional Convention, creating a House based on population and a Senate with equal representation. It resolved the dispute between the Virginia and New Jersey Plans. For 10 points, name this compromise.
In this 1787 essay James Madison argued that a large republic would control the dangers of faction. It is the best-known of the Federalist Papers. For 10 points, name this essay, numbered ten.

President John Adams sent diplomats to France in 1797, but agents later called X, Y, and Z demanded a bribe. The affair led to an undeclared naval conflict. For 10 points, name this diplomatic incident.

In this late 1814 meeting in Connecticut, Federalist delegates from New England discussed grievances over the War of 1812 and possibly secession. News of the Battle of New Orleans made them look unpatriotic. For 10 points, name this convention named for a city.

South Carolina declared the 1828 and 1832 tariffs void in this 1832 crisis. John C. Calhoun provided the theory, and Andrew Jackson threatened force. Henry Clay brokered a compromise tariff. For 10 points, name this crisis over states' rights.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized this 1848 gathering at a Wesleyan chapel, where Frederick Douglass spoke in favor of voting rights for women. Delegates signed a Declaration of Sentiments with eleven resolutions. For 10 points, name this first women's rights convention, held in a New York town.

In 1846 a Pennsylvania congressman proposed this amendment to a military appropriations bill to ban slavery in any land acquired from Mexico. The House passed it repeatedly but the Senate did not. For 10 points, name this proviso.

In 1858 Stephen Douglas defended popular sovereignty in debates against Abraham Lincoln across Illinois. At Freeport Douglas stated what became known as his Freeport Doctrine. For 10 points, name this series of debates in a Senate race.

On April 12, 1861 Confederate forces under P. G. T. Beauregard fired on this island fort in Charleston harbor. Major Robert Anderson surrendered after thirty-four hours. For 10 points, name this opening engagement of the Civil War.

In this deal after the disputed 1876 election, Democrats accepted Rutherford B. Hayes as president in return for the removal of federal troops from the South. It effectively ended Reconstruction. For 10 points, name this compromise.

In this 1896 case the Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented. The "separate but equal" doctrine came from it. For 10 points, name this case.
In 1894 Eugene V. Debs led the American Railway Union in this strike against a Chicago sleeping-car company. President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops. For 10 points, name this strike.

William Jennings Bryan electrified the 1896 Democratic convention with a speech opposing the gold standard. He said, "You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." For 10 points, name this speech.

This 1904 corollary to a doctrine stated that the United States could intervene in Latin America to prevent European intervention. Theodore Roosevelt used it regarding the Dominican Republic. For 10 points, name this corollary to the Monroe Doctrine.

In January 1917 Germany's foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a message to Mexico proposing an alliance. British intelligence intercepted it. For 10 points, name this telegram that helped bring the United States into World War I.

Two Italian immigrants were convicted of a 1920 robbery and murder in Massachusetts and executed in 1927. Their trial became a symbol of anti-immigrant bias and radical hysteria. For 10 points, name this pair, Nicola and Bartolomeo.

This 1930 act raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods. Economists blame it for deepening the Great Depression by prompting retaliation abroad. It was named for two Republican legislators. For 10 points, name this tariff law.
In 1932 about 17,000 World War I veterans camped in Washington, D.C., demanding early payment of bonuses. General Douglas MacArthur drove them out. For 10 points, name this protest group.

In this 1944 case the Supreme Court upheld the internment of Japanese Americans in a 6-3 decision. Justice Frank Murphy called the order racism. For 10 points, name this case, named for a man who defied the order.
This 1947 plan proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall gave billions of dollars in aid to rebuild Western Europe. The Soviet Union refused to participate. For 10 points, name this plan.

In 1950 this Wisconsin senator claimed he had a list of Communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings damaged him, and the Senate censured him in 1954. For 10 points, name this senator.

In August 1964 North Vietnamese boats allegedly attacked the USS Maddox in a gulf off Vietnam. Congress passed a resolution letting President Lyndon Johnson use force in Southeast Asia. For 10 points, name this resolution named for a body of water.

In this 1966 case the Supreme Court ruled that police must inform suspects of their rights to remain silent and have an attorney. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the opinion. For 10 points, name this case.

In 1978 President Jimmy Carter hosted Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menachem Begin at a presidential retreat in Maryland. The resulting agreements led to a 1979 peace treaty. For 10 points, name this series of agreements named for the retreat.
In this 1620 document signed aboard a ship off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims agreed to form a government and obey its laws. It was a precedent for self-government. For 10 points, name this compact.

This 1825 waterway linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie and lowered shipping costs to the Midwest. Governor DeWitt Clinton pushed for it, and critics called it "Clinton's Ditch." For 10 points, name this canal.

q: In January 1077 Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow for three days outside a fortress in northern Italy to seek forgiveness. Pope Gregory VII had excommunicated him during a dispute over who could appoint bishops. The fortress belonged to Matilda of Tuscany. For 10 points, name this castle whose name is a byword for submission to authority.

This 1204 crusade, supported by Venice under Doge Enrico Dandolo, never reached Egypt or the Holy Land. Instead its army sacked the capital of the Byzantine Empire. A Latin Empire was set up afterward. For 10 points, name this crusade numbered fourth.

From 1309 to 1377 the popes lived in this city in southern France instead of Rome. Clement V began the practice. The period was followed by the Western Schism. For 10 points, name this city, whose papal palace still stands.

This English dynastic conflict between the houses of Lancaster and York began in 1455. Richard III was killed at Bosworth Field in 1485, and Henry Tudor took the throne. For 10 points, name this series of civil wars named for flowers.

This Bohemian reformer and rector of Charles University was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance in 1415. His followers, the Hussites, fought crusades against them. He was inspired by John Wycliffe. For 10 points, name this man.

This Habsburg ruler was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain as Charles I. He presided over the Diet of Worms and abdicated in 1556, dividing his lands between his son and brother. For 10 points, name this ruler, numbered five.

In August 1572 Catholic mobs in Paris killed thousands of Huguenots after the wedding of Henry of Navarre to Margaret of Valois. Catherine de Medici is often blamed. The massacre is named for the feast day on which it began. For 10 points, name this massacre.

This nobleman, called "the Silent," led the Dutch Revolt against Spain's Philip II. He was a Prince of Orange and was assassinated in Delft in 1584. For 10 points, name this man, the great-grandfather of the later English king.

In 1571 a Holy League fleet defeated Ottoman forces in this naval battle in the Gulf of Patras. Don John of Austria commanded the Christian ships, and Miguel de Cervantes was wounded. For 10 points, name this battle.

This series of treaties of 1713 and 1714 ended the War of the Spanish Succession. Philip V kept the Spanish throne but renounced the French one. Britain gained Gibraltar and Minorca. For 10 points, name these treaties named for a Dutch city.

Frederick the Great of Prussia survived this global conflict of 1756 to 1763, known in America as the French and Indian War. The Treaty of Paris ended it, and Britain gained Canada. For 10 points, name this war named for its length.

In 1772, 1793, and 1795 Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided this country, which disappeared from the map until 1918. Tadeusz Kosciuszko led a failed uprising in 1794. For 10 points, name this country.

Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert edited this Enlightenment work, published from 1751 to 1772 in many volumes. It aimed to gather all knowledge and was opposed by the Church. For 10 points, name this French reference work.

In June 1789 the National Assembly's deputies met on an indoor court in Versailles and swore not to disband until they had written a constitution. Jacques-Louis David sketched it. For 10 points, name this oath.

On November 9, 1799, Napoleon Bonaparte and Emmanuel Sieyes overthrew the Directory in this coup. The date is by the revolutionary calendar. For 10 points, name this coup named for a month, which began the Consulate.

Horatio Nelson was killed at this 1805 naval battle off the coast of Spain. The British victory over a French and Spanish fleet ended Napoleon's invasion hopes. For 10 points, name this battle named for a cape.
In August 1819 cavalry charged a peaceful crowd demanding parliamentary reform in Manchester, killing about fifteen. The name mocks Waterloo. For 10 points, name this massacre at Saint Peter's Field.

This 1832 act in Britain eliminated rotten boroughs and gave seats to growing industrial cities like Manchester. Earl Grey was prime minister. For 10 points, name this first major electoral law of its kind in the nineteenth century.
This 1846 repeal of tariffs on imported grain was achieved by Robert Peel with help from Whigs and Richard Cobden. It split the Conservative Party. For 10 points, name this British legislation.

In May 1848 delegates met in Saint Paul's Church in this city to draft a constitution for a united Germany. They offered the crown to Frederick William IV of Prussia, who refused. For 10 points, name this assembly named for a city.
In 1894 a Jewish French army captain was falsely convicted of treason and sent to Devil's Island. Emile Zola wrote "J'Accuse" to defend him. For 10 points, name this scandal named for the captain.
This radical government ruled Paris in the spring of 1871 after France's defeat by Prussia. It was crushed in the "Bloody Week" by troops from Versailles. For 10 points, name this government.

The Schlieffen Plan called for Germany to defeat France quickly by marching through this neutral country. Its invasion in 1914 brought Britain into World War I. For 10 points, name this small country whose capital is Brussels.
From February to December 1916 the French and Germans fought this longest battle of World War I, around a fortress on the Meuse. Philippe Petain became a hero there. For 10 points, name this battle.
In 1923 Adolf Hitler and the Nazis tried to seize power in Munich by marching from a beer hall. The attempt failed and he was jailed. For 10 points, name this unsuccessful uprising.

Pablo Picasso painted this huge black-and-white canvas in 1937 for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the Paris World Exposition. It shows screaming figures, a bull, and a wounded horse. It responds to the German bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. For 10 points, name this painting.
In August 1939 Germany and the USSR signed this treaty, which contained a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe. It was named for two foreign ministers. For 10 points, name this pact.

In late May and early June 1940 hundreds of small civilian boats helped rescue over 300,000 British and French soldiers from a beach and harbor in northern France. German forces had trapped the army against the sea. Winston Churchill said that wars are not won by evacuations. For 10 points, name this evacuation.
In February 1945 Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin met at this Crimean resort to plan the postwar order. They agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones. For 10 points, name this conference.

In 1968 Alexander Dubcek introduced "socialism with a human face" in this country, but Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August. For 10 points, name this country and this reform period, called a "spring" in its capital.
This Polish electrician led the Solidarity movement at the Gdansk shipyard in 1980. He won the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize and became Poland's president in 1990. For 10 points, name this man.

q: Around 1200 BC groups known by this collective name, mentioned in Egyptian inscriptions at Medinet Habu, attacked the eastern Mediterranean. Ramses III repelled them. Their migrations coincided with the collapse of Ugarit and the Hittite Empire. For 10 points, name these raiders, whose label does not describe them as a single nation.

This Assyrian king assembled a library of clay tablets at Nineveh in the seventh century BC. It preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh. He fought a civil war against his brother in Babylon. For 10 points, name this last great king of Assyria.

This Lydian king, known for his wealth, was defeated by Cyrus the Great around 546 BC. He asked the oracle at Delphi whether he should attack Persia and was told a great empire would fall. For 10 points, name this man, whose name is a byword for wealth.

In 479 BC the Greek allies under the Spartan regent Pausanias crushed the last major Persian army on Greek soil at this battle in Boeotia. The Persian commander Mardonius died. For 10 points, name this land battle.
This Athenian reformer of 594 BC canceled debts, ended debt slavery, and divided citizens into four property classes. He is counted among the Seven Sages. For 10 points, name this lawgiver.

In 371 BC this Theban general broke Sparta's reputation for invincibility at Leuctra using an oblique formation. He also freed the Messenian helots. He died at Mantinea in 362. For 10 points, name this man.

In 338 BC this king of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea. He had reformed the army with the long pike called the sarissa. He was assassinated in 336 by one of his bodyguards. For 10 points, name this father of Alexander.
This Epirote king won costly battles against Rome at Heraclea and Asculum in the 270s BC. His name gives us a phrase for a victory that costs too much. For 10 points, name this king.
In 202 BC the Romans under Scipio defeated Hannibal at this battle near Carthage. Masinissa's Numidian cavalry helped. It ended the Second Punic War. For 10 points, name this battle.

These two brothers, tribunes of the plebs in the 130s and 120s BC, proposed land reforms and were killed by senatorial mobs. Their opponents included Scipio Nasica, who led senators wielding stool legs against Tiberius. Their mother Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus. For 10 points, name these Roman reformers.

This Roman general reformed the army in 107 BC by recruiting landless citizens and held the consulship seven times. His rival Sulla marched on Rome. For 10 points, name this uncle of Julius Caesar by marriage.
This Roman dictator in 82 BC issued proscription lists to eliminate enemies. He retired in 79 BC. He was first to march on Rome with an army. For 10 points, name this man who defeated Marius.
Crassus died in 53 BC in this disastrous battle against Parthian cavalry and horse archers in Mesopotamia. The Romans lost their legionary standards. For 10 points, name this battle.

In 48 BC Julius Caesar defeated Pompey at this battle in Greece. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was killed. Caesar had about half as many men as his rival, and his troops broke the cavalry on the enemy flank. The battle took place on a plain near the Enipeus River. For 10 points, name this battle in Thessaly.
In AD 9 Arminius ambushed three Roman legions led by Publius Quinctilius Varus in this German woodland. Augustus is said to have cried, "Give me back my legions!" For 10 points, name this battle.
This queen of the Iceni led a revolt against Rome in AD 60 or 61. She burned Londinium and Camulodunum. She was defeated by Suetonius Paulinus. For 10 points, name this British queen.

This Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher wrote the Meditations while on campaign along the Danube. He was the last of the "Five Good Emperors." His son Commodus succeeded him. For 10 points, name this man.

In AD 212 an emperor of the Severan dynasty issued an edict extending Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. He killed his brother Geta. For 10 points, name this emperor, for whom a famous set of baths in Rome is named.

In AD 378 Emperor Valens was killed at this battle in Thrace by Gothic cavalry. It showed the weakness of the Roman army. The emperor had refused to wait for reinforcements from his nephew Gratian. Two-thirds of the eastern field army perished in the fighting. For 10 points, name this battle named for a city.

In 451 the Romans and Visigoths under Aetius defeated this ruler of the Huns on the Catalaunian Plains. He later invaded Italy and was turned back from Rome. For 10 points, name this "Scourge of God."

In AD 476 this Germanic general deposed the last western Roman emperor Romulus Augustulus. He ruled Italy as king. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and nominally accepted the authority of Emperor Zeno. The deposed boy emperor was pensioned off in Campania. For 10 points, name this man.

This dynasty ruled much of the Yellow River valley from around 1600 BC. Its kings used oracle bones for divination and buried chariots in royal tombs at Anyang. For 10 points, name this dynasty that preceded the Zhou.

The Zhou kings justified overthrowing the Shang with this doctrine, saying that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler. The idea was used by the Duke of Zhou to defend the conquest of King Wu. It was later applied to explain the rise and fall of later dynasties, which supposedly lost it through misrule. For 10 points, name this Chinese concept.

This Chinese general and strategist, said to have served the state of Wu, wrote a treatise on war containing the line "all warfare is based on deception." For 10 points, name this author of The Art of War.

This Han emperor ruled from 141 to 87 BC, expanded Chinese territory, sent Zhang Qian west, and established Confucianism as state doctrine. For 10 points, name this emperor whose name means "martial."

This Bronze Age city in the Indus Valley had a Great Bath, a grid plan, and drains. It was excavated in the 1920s in what is now Pakistan. For 10 points, name this city whose name means "mound of the dead."

This founder of the Mauryan Empire took power around 321 BC after the Nanda dynasty. He later became a Jain monk. His adviser Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra. For 10 points, name this emperor, grandfather of Ashoka.
This capital of the Assyrian Empire on the Tigris was destroyed in 612 BC by a Babylonian and Median alliance. It lies across the river from modern Mosul. For 10 points, name this city.

q: In 216 BC the consuls Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus led about 80,000 Romans against a smaller army in Apulia. Hannibal placed weaker Gallic and Spanish infantry in the center and let the Roman legions be surrounded by his cavalry and African infantry. Paullus died in the fighting. For 10 points, name this battle, a model of double envelopment.

In 331 BC Alexander the Great met the army of Darius III on a plain east of the Tigris. Scythed chariots failed against his phalanx, and Alexander led a cavalry charge at a gap in the enemy line. Darius fled and was later killed by Bessus. For 10 points, name this decisive battle that ended the Achaemenid Empire.

In 755 this general rebelled against the Tang court at the capital of Chang'an, nearly toppling the dynasty. He had been a favorite of Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei. For 10 points, name this rebel, whose name is An.

This Song dynasty chancellor, who served Emperor Shenzong, tried to reform government with measures like the Green Sprouts law. Conservatives under Sima Guang opposed him. For 10 points, name this statesman.
This Japanese novel, written around 1000 by a court lady, follows a prince in the Heian court. It is often called the world's first novel. For 10 points, name this work by Murasaki Shikibu.
In 1185 this man of the Minamoto clan defeated the Taira at Dan-no-ura and became the first shogun in 1192 of the Kamakura shogunate. His wife was Hojo Masako. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1260 the Mamluks under Baibars and Qutuz defeated a Mongol army at this battle in Palestine. It halted Mongol expansion into Egypt. For 10 points, name this battle whose name means "Spring of Goliath."
This Turco-Mongol conqueror, called "the Lame," built an empire from Samarkand around 1370 to 1405. He captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid at Ankara in 1402. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1526 Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at this battle north of Delhi, founding the Mughal Empire. He used gunpowder and cannon. The Mughal victory was helped by field artillery, which Ottoman advisers had taught Babur to use. The sultan of Delhi died on the field and the battle was fought on a plain. For 10 points, name this battle.

In 1514 the Ottomans under Selim I used cannon and muskets to defeat the Safavid Shah Ismail at this battle in eastern Anatolia. The Safavid cavalry lacked firearms and could not break the Ottoman janissaries behind wagons and cannon. Selim then briefly occupied Tabriz. For 10 points, name this battle.

This Safavid shah, who ruled from 1588 to 1629, moved the capital to Isfahan and defeated the Uzbeks and Ottomans. He is called "the Great." He used English adventurers like Robert Sherley to modernize his army with artillery. He also settled Armenian merchants in New Julfa near his new capital. For 10 points, name this ruler.

In 1757 Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah at this battle in Bengal, helping establish East India Company rule. Clive had bribed the nawab's commander Mir Jafar to stay out of the fight. The nawab was later captured and killed, and Mir Jafar was installed. For 10 points, name this battle.
This Mughal emperor ruled from 1658 to 1707, expanded to the Deccan, and reimposed the jizya. His wars with the Marathas strained the empire. For 10 points, name this son of Shah Jahan.

This Maratha ruler carved out a Hindu kingdom in western India and was crowned chhatrapati in 1674. He fought Aurangzeb using guerrilla tactics. He escaped from Agra by hiding in a basket of sweets after being summoned by the Mughal emperor. He built a navy and many hill forts, such as Raigad. For 10 points, name this man.

This southern African stone city, built from the eleventh to fifteenth centuries by the Shona, has a Great Enclosure. Its name means "stone houses." For 10 points, name this site, which gave a modern country its name.
This queen of Ndongo and Matamba in Angola resisted Portuguese slave traders in the seventeenth century. She negotiated with Portugal and allied with the Dutch. For 10 points, name this woman.

In 1896 Ethiopian forces under Menelik II defeated an Italian army at this battle, preserving Ethiopian independence. The Italians had advanced in separate columns that lost contact, and about 70,000 Ethiopian soldiers overwhelmed them. Empress Taytu also took part in the campaign. For 10 points, name this battle in the Tigray highlands.
In 1898 Herbert Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army defeated the Mahdist forces of the Khalifa at this battle in Sudan. Winston Churchill took part as a cavalry officer. For 10 points, name this battle.
